THREE

What the River Kept

The river had moved twice in living memory, and both times it had taken something with it that the town had not been ready to give. The first time it was the mill, which had stood on the old bank for two hundred years and was found one spring morning standing in a field, a quarter of a mile from any water, with its wheel turning slowly in the wind as if it had not yet noticed what had happened.1

The second time it was the ferry, and the ferryman, who had refused to believe that a river could change its mind and had gone on waiting at the old landing for three days with his lantern lit. People brought him food and blankets and told him the news, and he thanked them politely and went on waiting, and on the fourth morning he was gone and so was the boat.

Nobody in the town talked about the ferryman after that, at least not where children could hear, and so of course the children talked about nothing else. They said he had rowed out to find where the river had gone, and that on quiet nights you could still see his lantern moving along the old bed, looking for the water that had left him behind.

1. The mill still stands.
